newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Council agrees access to justice system.
newsitem.headline: Council agrees access to justice system.

text.p: The Consumer Affairs Council on Thursday struck a common position on the directive on injunctions for the protection of consumer interests after difficult negotiations with Germany and Britain.

Under the accord, aggrieved consumers throughout the European Union will be able to seek redress in all the 15 member states via recognised national consumer organisations or ombudsmen, under a principle of mutual recognition.
Industrial and commercial organisations are not included in the scope of organisations deemed able to represent consumers.
The organisations will be able to press claims for breaches of all nine EU consumer directives on the statute book.
Consumer Affairs Commissioner Emma Bonino told a news conference the accord was a milestone and a "change of philosophy" in consumer rights.

Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Anneke van Dok van Weele, who presided the meeting, said the accord had been difficult to reach because it required some countries -- notably Germany and Britain -- to change their ways.
"It has been difficult because it does require change and a measure of harmonisation in the member states," she told the news conference.

At the end of the meeting Germany, which wanted to limit the accord's scope to four EU directives rather than nine, was still opposed to the legislation, but that will not prevent formal adooption by the others.
Britain had held out against the directive because it has a unique two week period in which complaints are cleared before going to a consumer body.
Lack of redress in consumer problems has been seen as a barrier to the real success of the EU's single market as people have been afraid to buy outside their own country.
